props.title: The Car

sections.content: The Car (1977) stands as a fascinating entry in the demonic vehicle subgenre that emerged in the wake of Duel (1971) and Christine (1983). Director Elliot Silverstein crafts a supernatural thriller where a mysterious black Lincoln Continental terrorizes a small Utah town. The film cleverly builds on the success of Jaws (1975), essentially transplanting the unstoppable predator concept from ocean to desert. What sets it apart is its explicit supernatural elements - the car can't cross hallowed ground and appears seemingly invincible, suggesting demonic possession rather than just a murderous driver.

sections.content: The late 1970s and early 1980s saw a fascinating wave of killer vehicle films that tapped into growing anxieties about technology and automation. The Car arrived alongside films like Race with the Devil (1975) and Death Car on the Freeway (1979), reflecting Cold War-era fears about loss of control and mechanical menace. The film's desert setting proves particularly effective, with the vast empty landscapes emphasizing human vulnerability against the unstoppable machine.

James Brolin's performance as Deputy Wade Parent grounds the supernatural elements in believable human drama, following a template that would later influence films like Joy Ride (2001) and Jeepers Creepers (1999). The Car itself, designed by George Barris (famous for the 1966 Batmobile), became an iconic movie vehicle, with its modified 1971 Lincoln Continental Mark III embodying mechanical malevolence through clever design choices like the lack of visible door handles and blacked-out windows. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond just automotive horror. Its blend of supernatural horror with action sequences helped pave the way for genre hybrids like The Wraith (1986) and Highway to Hell (1991). Modern films like Death Proof (2007) and Monster Trucks (2016) continue to draw from its playbook of vehicular terror, though few match its commitment to presenting the car as a purely supernatural entity rather than a tool of human malice.
